what: Colossus Mark 1, a programmable (plugs and switches) electronic valve machine, performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill (GPO research station, London) under Tommy Flowers.

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It performed satisfactorily at Dollis Hill on 8 December 1943

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: Colossus is regarded as the world's first programmable, electronic, digital computer.

note: Earlier candidates: Atanasoff-Berry computer (tested 1942) is electronic but not programmable; Zuse Z3 (May 1941) is programmable but electromechanical relays. Later and stricter readings: ENIAC (general-purpose, Dec 1945 / dedicated Feb 1946) and Manchester Baby (first stored-program, 21 June 1948). Colossus is not stored-program and was special-purpose, so fit to 'stores data and runs programs' is partial. The first pass (ENIAC 1945) was later.

what: Colossus Mark 1, installed at Bletchley Park, attacked its first Lorenz-cipher message (processing intercepted traffic for the Allies).

sources.title: Colossus computer
sources.quote: It was operational in January and it successfully attacked its first message on 5 February 1944.

note: Delivered to Bletchley 18 Jan 1944 and operational that month; first real message 5 Feb 1944. Rejected as earlier: ABC (never used for real work). ENIAC's first real program (Dec 1945) is later.

what: Sir William Thomson's tide-predicting machine (built 1872-73 by Alexander Legé, with Edward Roberts); a model was exhibited at the British Association meeting, 1873.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: A model of it was exhibited at the British Association meeting in 1873

note: Judged on mechanism: continuous mechanical quantities (pulleys and cranks) summing harmonic terms, i.e. it models an equation, but it evaluates a fixed formula rather than solving general equations. If the definition is read strictly as 'solves differential equations', the earliest working machine is Bush's MIT differential analyzer (1928-31, first pass), with Hartree's Manchester model 1934. James Thomson's 1876 integrating machine was a description, not a working solver. Rejected as loose analogues: planimeters, astrolabe and the Antikythera mechanism (c.150-100 BC, an orrery, not an equation solver).

what: A larger tide-predicting machine (20 components) was built for the Government of India and used to generate tide data for Indian ports.

sources.title: Tide-predicting machine
sources.quote: An enlarged and improved version of the machine, for computing 20 tidal components, was built for the Government of India in 1879

note: The 1876 ten-component machine may have produced earlier tide tables but no use date was found. Arthur Pollen's naval fire-control analog computer (c.1912) and Bush's differential analyzer (1931, used operationally in the 1930s) are later.

what: Herman Hollerith's first tabulators compiled mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City (trial of the card-and-counter system).

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's first tabulators were used to compile mortality statistics for Baltimore, Jersey City and New York City in 1886.

note: Wikipedia says 1886; other histories (Smithsonian, Franklin Institute, USPTO, per search summaries I could not fetch) put the Baltimore trial in 1887, so the date may be 1887. Hollerith's patent application was filed 1884 but described a concept. Earlier punched-card machines (Jacquard 1804, Korsakov 1832 proposal) do not tabulate, count or sort records, so were rejected.

what: Hollerith electric tabulators compiled the 1890 US Census from about 100 million punched cards.

sources.title: Tabulating machine
sources.quote: Hollerith's method was used for the 1890 census.

note: The 1886/87 Baltimore mortality work was a trial; the 1890 census was the first large-scale official deployment. If the mortality compilation is counted as real use, the date would be 1886-87.

what: The Banu Musa brothers in Baghdad described an automatic flute player driven by a pinned barrel, in their Book of Ingenious Devices (c. 850).

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: credited with inventing the first music sequencer, as described in the manuscript, as an example of an early type of programmable machine.

sources.title: Banu Musa
sources.quote: a Persian family of polymaths, astronomers, mathematicians, and engineers active in 9th century Baghdad

note: Date is approximate (the book is conventionally dated c. 850; the page says only 9th century). Pinned-barrel machine plays a recorded sequence without an operator, so mechanism fits, though the page hedges ('may have been the first programmable machine'). Earlier: Hellenistic automata (e.g. Hero) not checked. The first pass (1952 MIT numerical control) and Jacquard 1804 are later.

what: Basile Bouchon, a silk-weaving worker in Lyon, controlled a drawloom with a perforated paper roll.

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: invented a way to control a loom with a perforated paper roll in 1725

sources.title: Basile Bouchon
sources.quote: This development is considered to be the first industrial application of a semi-automated machine.

note: Bouchon's loom still needed an extra operator, so it is only partly 'rather than by an operator'. Falcon 1728, Vaucanson 1745 and Jacquard (patent 1804, 'wildly successful' 1805) refined it; Jacquard is the first fully card-driven loom in wide use. Musical automata with pinned barrels (c. 850 on) were pleasure devices, not production use.

what: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments demonstrated the first working integrated circuit (germanium, wire-bonded).

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: successfully demonstrating the first working example of an integrated circuit on 12 September 1958

sources.title: Q80831
sources.quote: time of discovery or invention (P575): 1958

note: Earlier ideas considered: Jacobi's 1949 patent and Dummer's 1952 concept (concepts, no working circuit found); micromodules (1957) were assembled discrete parts. Noyce's monolithic planar IC followed about six months later.

what: Integrated circuits entered use in products and in the US space and military programs; NASA's Apollo program was the largest single consumer 1961-65.

sources.title: Integrated circuit
sources.quote: NASA's Apollo Program was the largest single consumer of integrated circuits between 1961 and 1965.

note: Date is inferred from the start of the 1961-65 consumption window; I did not confirm the first commercial IC sale (Texas Instruments/Fairchild, c. 1960-61), which may be slightly earlier. No earlier use of Kilby's 1958 prototype found.

what: General Electric built a demonstration computer from thin-film cryotrons (arrays of 2000 devices operated), following John Bremer's 1957 planar cryotron.

sources.title: Cryotron
sources.quote: In the next few years, a demonstration computer was made and arrays with 2000 devices operated.

note: The page gives only 'the next few years' after 1957, so the year 1960 is approximate (1958-1961). Buck's 1953-55 cryotron was a single switching element, not a computer. No machine described as a working superconducting computer was found in other sources. No practical use: cryotron work was abandoned by the mid-1960s and, per Wikipedia, there are no commercial superconducting computers as of 2016. No mass adoption.

what: Valdemar Poulsen invented the Telegraphone, the first magnetic recorder (steel wire); he demonstrated it at the 1900 Paris Exposition.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: The first crude magnetic recorder was invented in 1898 by Valdemar Poulsen.

note: Earlier: Oberlin Smith's 1888 Electrical World article proposed wire recording but no working machine is recorded. The definition includes sound, so the audio telegraphone counts. Later: tape 1928 (Pfleumer), drum 1932 (Tauschek), RAMAC disk 1956 (first pass).

what: The American Telegraphone Company of Springfield, Massachusetts manufactured the Telegraphone, the first commercially available magnetic recorder, for dictation and telephone recording.

sources.title: Wire recording
sources.quote: manufactured by the American Telegraphone Company, Springfield, Massachusetts in 1903

note: Page says use was 'extremely limited' through the 1920s-30s. Earlier practical use (e.g. the 1900 Paris demonstration recording of Franz Josef) was a demonstration. Digital data use began later with UNIVAC I tape (1951) and RAMAC (1956). mass_adoption left out: the page says affordable tape recorders for home and office appeared in the first half of the 1950s but gives no firm year.

what: John Benjamin Dancer produced microphotographs (daguerreotype images reduced 160:1), viewed through a microscope.

sources.title: Microphotography
sources.quote: John Benjamin Dancer was one of the first to produce microphotographs, in 1839.

note: Dancer's work was a novelty with no document-storage purpose; the idea of microphotography for preserving documents was first suggested by Glaisher in 1851 and Herschel in 1853. Fit to 'books and records on film read through a viewer' is loose, as the first pass said. Rene Dagron's 1859 patent and Otlet's 1906 microphotographic book are later.

what: During the Siege of Paris, Rene Dagron microphotographed dispatches on thin collodion film; carried by pigeon, they were projected by magic lantern and transcribed.

sources.title: Microform
sources.quote: By 28 January 1871, when Paris and the Government of National Defense surrendered, Dagron had delivered 115,000 messages to Paris by carrier pigeon.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Recordak 1928, bank cheques; page says commercial use began in the 1920s with McCarthy's 1925 Checkograph). The pigeon-post films carried messages and newspaper pages, a close match to records on film read through a projector.

what: Marvin Minsky and Dean Edmonds built SNARC (40 vacuum-tube neurons, Navy-funded) at Princeton; it learned to solve a maze.

sources.title: SNARC
sources.quote: They tested the machine on a copy of Shannon's maze, and found that it could learn to solve the maze.

sources.title: Marvin Minsky
sources.quote: In 1951, Minsky built SNARC, which is often considered the first artificial neural network.

note: Earlier than the first pass (Rosenblatt's perceptron 1957-58). McCulloch and Pitts (1943) was a non-learning mathematical model, not a built machine; Farley and Clark (1954) simulated a Hebbian network on a computer, later than SNARC. Exact month of SNARC working not found (funded summer 1951).

what: Bell Labs applied convolutional neural networks trained by backpropagation (LeNet) to handwritten digit recognition for zip codes, later reading cheques in ATMs.

sources.title: LeNet
sources.quote: In 1989, Yann LeCun et al. at Bell Labs first applied the backpropagation algorithm to practical applications

note: Widrow and Hoff's ADALINE (1960) and MADALINE (largest built 1963) adaptive filters are described by Wikipedia as 'likely the first artificial neural network applied to a real-world problem' (phone-line echo removal), which would be earlier, but I found no dated first deployment. The CIA studied the Mark I Perceptron 1960-64 only as an evaluation.

what: Google Translate switched to the neural machine translation system GNMT in November 2016, putting neural networks in daily use by very large numbers of ordinary people.

sources.title: Google Neural Machine Translation
sources.quote: In November 2016, Google Neural Machine Translation system (GNMT) was introduced.

note: Year is a judgment: ordinary people used neural networks unknowingly earlier (cheque reading from the 1990s, speech recognition from the early 2010s) and no source states when use became routine.

what: Leonard Adleman (USC) solved a seven-node directed Hamiltonian path problem using DNA molecules in a test tube.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: Adleman demonstrated a proof-of-concept use of DNA as a form of computation which solved the seven-point Hamiltonian path problem.

sources.title: DNA computing
sources.quote: the field originally started with the demonstration of a computing application by Leonard Adleman in 1994

note: No earlier computation by living cells or organic chemistry in a deliberately built computer was found; later demonstrations include DNA walkers (2003) and 3-SAT with 20 variables (2002). Publication month (Science, Nov 1994) is from the first pass, not confirmed here. No practical use or mass adoption: still laboratory research.

what: Texas Instruments' 'Cal Tech' prototype, led by Jack Kilby, was the first handheld electronic calculator (paper-tape output).

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first handheld calculator was a 1967 prototype called Cal Tech

note: Earlier: the Curta (1947) was a mechanical, not electronic and not battery-powered. Desktop electronic calculators from 1961 (ANITA) were too big to be pocket devices. Wikidata gives only 'start time: 1960s' for 'calculator'.

what: The first commercially produced portable electronic calculators (Sanyo ICC-0081, Canon Pocketronic, Sharp QT-8B) appeared in Japan.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: The first commercially produced portable calculators appeared in Japan in 1970

note: Earlier than the first pass (Bowmar 1971, HP-35 1972). Sharp EL-8 (Jan 1971) was close to pocket size. Exact 1970 month not given.

what: Pocket electronic calculators became popular as integrated circuits cut their size and cost.

sources.title: Calculator
sources.quote: They became popular in the mid-1970s as the incorporation of integrated circuits reduced their size and cost.

note: 'Mid-1970s' is the source's wording; 1975 is my choice of year.

what: John Blankenbaker designed the Kenbak-1, a TTL-logic 8-bit computer intended for individuals and schools.

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: Designed in 1970 by John Blankenbaker

note: Date is the design year; no exact date of a working prototype was found. Rejected as earlier: Wikidata's 1957 (IBM 610 Auto-Point was single-operator but a costly office machine), LINC (1962, a laboratory minicomputer), Olivetti Programma 101 (1965, programmable calculator) and Datapoint 2200 (June 1970, a terminal). The Computer History Museum, per Wikipedia, calls the Kenbak-1 the first personal computer.

what: The Kenbak-1 went on sale in early 1971 at about $750 (fewer than 50 built).

sources.title: Kenbak-1
sources.quote: was first sold in early 1971

note: Earlier than the first pass (Altair 8800, Jan 1975). Micral N (early 1973) was the first microprocessor-based PC. Very few units sold, so use was marginal.

what: Commodore PET (announced Jan 1977), Apple II (shipped 10 June 1977) and TRS-80 (1977) were the first mass-marketed personal computers.

sources.title: History of personal computers
sources.quote: The first successfully mass-marketed personal computer to be announced was the Commodore PET after being revealed in January 1977.

note: 1977 is when mass-market sales began; routine household use came during the 1980s (IBM PC 1981 onward), which I did not date from a source.

what: Psion launched the Organiser, a pocket computer with a one-line LCD and database; Wikipedia calls it the 'world's first practical pocket computer'.

sources.title: Psion Organiser
sources.quote: Launched in 1984,  the Psion Organiser was the "world's first practical pocket computer".

note: Same event as first_practical_use. Earlier candidates: Pitroda's 1975 electronic diary patent (no device found); Sharp PC-1211 pocket computer (March 1980, a programmable computer, not a notes/schedule device); Thorp and Shannon's 1961 shoe roulette computer (not a notes device). Organiser II (1986) is the first 'usable' PDA per Wikipedia.

what: Psion Organiser sold in the UK as a pocket diary and database computer.

sources.title: Personal digital assistant
sources.quote: The first PDA, the Organiser, was released in 1984 by Psion

note: Same date as demonstration; the Organiser I was a commercial product from the start.

what: Palm's PalmPilot handhelds (first Palm line March 1996, PalmPilot March 1997) reportedly sold over a million units by 1998.

sources.title: PalmPilot
sources.quote: PalmPilot had reportedly sold over 1 million units by 1998.

note: The page gives a sales figure rather than a 'became common' date, so 1998 is a judgment; Apple Newton (1993) sold poorly.

what: IBM presented the Naval Ordnance Research Calculator (NORC) to the US Navy; at the ceremony it calculated pi to 3,089 digits in 13 minutes.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: At the presentation ceremony, it calculated pi to 3,089 digits, which was a record at the time.

note: NORC was 'likely the most powerful computer at the time' but is not usually called a supercomputer, so fit is uncertain. Later contenders: UNIVAC LARC (delivered June 1960), IBM 7030 Stretch (1961), Atlas (1962), CDC 6600 (1964, first pass 1965).

what: NORC moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia and was the main computer there (ballistics and ordnance calculations) until 1958.

sources.title: IBM NORC
sources.quote: In 1955, NORC was moved to the Naval Proving Ground at Dahlgren, Virginia. It was their main computer until 1958

note: It went into service December 1954 at the Watson laboratory; 1955 Dahlgren is the clear working deployment. LARC delivery to Livermore (June 1960) is later.

what: ENIAC was used for calculations of thermonuclear reactions for Los Alamos, its first program.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: In December 1945, the ENIAC was used to calculate thermonuclear reactions.

sources.title: Computer simulation
sources.quote: its first large-scale deployment during the Manhattan Project in World War II to model the process of nuclear detonation

note: Earlier than the first pass (ENIAC Monte Carlo, spring 1948, 'first fully automated Monte Carlo calculations'). Wikipedia dates the first large-scale computer simulation to the Manhattan Project (1944-45, by punched-card machines) but I did not confirm a date or a computer. Whether the Dec 1945 run counts as a model simulation rather than a calculation is a judgment; the 1944 Cambridge differential-analyzer simulations of transmission lines are not a first.

what: The same ENIAC run served Los Alamos hydrogen-bomb feasibility research.

sources.title: ENIAC
sources.quote: its first program was a study of the feasibility of the thermonuclear weapon

note: Same event as first_demonstration. Monte Carlo neutron-diffusion simulations followed in spring 1948 (Von Neumann, Metropolis).

concept_note: Moved earlier than first pass (ENIAC 1945) to Colossus (Dec 1943 / Feb 1944) because Colossus was a working programmable electronic machine; fit is partial since it was not stored-program. No mass_adoption: mainframes were not used routinely by ordinary people (UNIVAC's 1952 election night raised awareness only).

First pass (1931 MIT differential analyzer) was too late if tide-predicting machines count (1873); low confidence because they sum harmonics rather than solve general equations. Mass adoption none: analog computers served specialists.
Added the Baltimore-era trial (1886, vs 1887 elsewhere) as demonstration and kept 1890 census as practical use. No mass_adoption: business and government equipment, not used by ordinary people.

Moved much earlier than the first pass (1952 NC): pinned-barrel and perforated-roll machines (c. 850; 1725) fit the definition. Both low. No mass_adoption: Jacquard looms and NC were industrial tools.
Demonstration confirmed (Kilby 1958); added practical use 1961 (low). No mass_adoption milestone: ICs became ubiquitous in products, but no sourced year.

First pass had none; Wikipedia says GE built a cryotron demonstration computer after 1957, year approximate. No practical use (cryotron work abandoned; no commercial superconducting computer as of 2016) and no mass adoption.
Moved to 1898 (Poulsen) and 1903 commercial Telegraphone from RAMAC 1956. No mass_adoption year found (home tape recorders in early 1950s).
Kept Dancer 1839 as low-confidence demonstration; practical use moved from 1928 Recordak to 1870 Dagron pigeon-post microfilm. No mass_adoption sourced.
Moved demonstration from Perceptron (1958) to SNARC (1951); added practical use (LeNet 1989, low) and mass adoption (2016, low).
Adleman 1994 confirmed as earliest; no practical use or mass adoption (laboratory research only).
Moved demonstration to 1967 Cal Tech prototype and practical use to 1970 (first pass said Bowmar 1971); added mass adoption mid-1970s.
Moved earlier than first pass (Altair 1975) to Kenbak-1 (1970/71); mass adoption kept at 1977.
Psion Organiser 1984 kept as earliest (demonstration and practical use same event, low); mass adoption set at 1998 from PalmPilot sales instead of 1996.
Moved earlier than first pass (CDC 6600, 1965) to IBM NORC (1954-55), low confidence because NORC is rarely called a supercomputer. No mass_adoption.
First pass had none; ENIAC Dec 1945 and Monte Carlo 1948 found. No mass_adoption sourced.

_tools: page_text worked for Wikipedia only (slow, rate-limited at times; all 38 quotes passed --check); non-Wikipedia hosts (Smithsonian, Franklin Institute, USPTO, Britannica, CHM) timed out or returned 403/proxy refusals so all sources are Wikipedia reference pages plus one Wikidata statement; WebSearch worked for summaries only; chronam and WebFetch not used.
